issues.title: [Russia] Censor has a new method of blocking
issues.body:
### Problem
A few weeks ago, a new method of blocking (especially on mobile networks) was introduced in Russia by the censor.
It works as follows. So, if:
1. The client connects to the server via TCP using HTTPS and TLS 1.3 (for example, VLESS/Reality actually mimics HTTPS with TLS 1.3);
2. The IP address of the server is “suspicious” (it is located **outside** ⚠️ (i.e. not in Russia), is part of the subnet AS which is owned by foreign data centers like Hetzner, Digital Ocean, etc.);
3. Within one TCP connection (not within one HTTP request/response - this is important) the data size received from the server to the client is more than ≈15-20KB (the value varies depending on the provider) — the MAIN thing.

This connection is "frozen" (i.e. TCP packets from the server within this connection stop arriving after the specified limit on the size of transmitted data has been reached). It is curious to note that, as a rule, the censor (under the pretence of a response from the server) does not send, for example, an RST packet - instead, it simply “freezes” the TCP connection (from the client's point of view), and thus the client simply waits for an error on the timeout of waiting for a response from the server and everything stops working.

**IMPORTANT**: It doesn't matter whether it's "legitimate" HTTPS traffic or whether someone is mimicking it. They don't pay attention to that now.

### Do I have these limitations?
You can check your “home” ISP with the _RU :: TCP 16-20_ checker from [this](https://github.com/hyperion-cs/dpi-checkers) repository. Works right from your browser, VPN should be disabled during the check.


### Notes
The good news is that if you fragment the responses from the server into several ≈15-20KB data bundles (if it is large enough) in different TCP connections, everything will work fine. It is important not to confuse this with fragmentation of TCP packets within one connection or splitting of transmitted data into several HTTP requests/responses (in **one** connection) - this is different and it won't help.

Yes, it will work noticeably slower than a single connection (especially if we're going to upload/download a large file). For example, it would take ~2560 TCP connections to download a 50MB file - that's a lot and quite suspicious. 

---

upd1: TLS 1.2 is also blocked (sometimes there is a different data size limit per TCP connection).

upd2: At the moment it seems that only SSH/sFTP + and sometimes RDP (both on any ports) work within TCP without limitations. Including random data transfer over TCP (without TLS, etc., in raw form) is also limited. It's possible that there are other things within TCP that would work without limitations, I'm not exactly sure about that.

upd3.: Censor has a whitelist (based on SNI in the TLS handshake and possibly an HTTP `Host` header if _plain HTTP_ is used), for more details, including some subset of that list, see [here](https://github.com/hyperion-cs/dpi-checkers/tree/main/ru/tcp-16-20_dwc). For example, this can be used as SNI/dest in xray/vless+reality (with _xtls-rprx-vision_) and it will work.

upd4.: ❗️Censor has also started to apply a whitelist based on the CIDR (IP subnets) of the destination servers. In this case, circumvention is extremely difficult (as a rule, an intermediate node with an IP from the whitelist is required).

upd5.: In fact, the censor typically freezes the connection after 25 packets have been sent in either direction (incoming/outgoing). This applies to both tcp and udp. On average, this equates to approximately 16 KB of payload.

### Related links
- https://blog.cloudflare.com/russian-internet-users-are-unable-to-access-the-open-internet/
- https://hyperion-cs.github.io/dpi-checkers/ru/tcp-16-20/
- https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/4835#issuecomment-2988824955
- https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/4846

issues.title: OSTP: an AI-assisted Rust tunnel that works in Russia — UDP gets blocked on mobile, real TLS gets through. Looking for review
issues.body:
Yes, this is another AI-assisted protocol (written with a lot of help from
Claude Code). But it works: it gets my relatives through censorship every day
and saves them a fair amount of money and nerves. Now I'd like people who know
DPI better than I do to tell me where the design breaks.

https://github.com/ospab/ostp — AGPL-3.0: the protocol, server, CLI, desktop and
Android apps.

### Wire image

- Handshake: `Noise_NNpsk0_25519_ChaChaPoly_BLAKE2s`; data: ChaCha20-Poly1305.
  Every secret is HKDF-derived from the shared access key. No custom primitives.
- No cleartext version field or magic byte. The 12-byte outer header (session id
  + nonce) is XOR-masked with HMAC-SHA256(obfuscation key, first 32 bytes of the
  packet's ciphertext), so headers are uncorrelated between packets.
- Handshake padding length is drawn from a range derived from the access key, so
  different deployments have different size distributions.
- Optional junk datagrams before the handshake (per-key marker, not a constant)
  and fragmentation of the first TCP write into small chunks.
- An unauthenticated peer gets a fallback website or a decoy, not a reset.

Spec: `docs/en/specification.md`, obfuscation: `docs/en/obfuscation.md`.

### Three carriers for the same datagrams

1. **UDP** — random-looking, own ARQ (selective ACK/NACK) and congestion control.
2. **UoT** — the same datagrams over plain TCP, for networks that throttle unknown UDP.
3. **TLS on 443** (added recently) — UoT inside real TLS with a real Let's Encrypt
   certificate on your domain, directly or behind nginx/Caddy on a secret path.
   Not an imitation: the server is a real website.

### What I've seen in Russia

- **My home (wired) ISP:** almost everything is blocked. OSTP works, and so does
  a carefully tuned VLESS setup; nothing else I tried does.
- **Mobile operators differ a lot.** On MegaFon, one of the biggest, VLESS
  surprisingly isn't blocked, but OSTP over plain UDP and over UoT are blocked
  readily. With UDP the client's counters show only a few hundred bytes coming
  back, and the handshake never completes or the session never becomes stable.
- **TLS works on both** the home ISP and MegaFon.

So in practice the "looks like nothing" carriers are what fails on mobile, and
the real-TLS carrier is what survives.

### What I know is weak

- UDP and UoT are fully encrypted protocols by design, so they're exposed to FEP
  blocking (entropy / "looks like nothing" heuristics) and whitelisting — the
  MegaFon result above is consistent with that.
- Length padding changes sizes but, as far as I can tell, doesn't hide the
  direction/count pattern from #363 (client sends ≥3 packets ≥411 bytes while
  the server talks more often) inside the TLS carrier.
- One developer, no audit.
- The repo has a prober (`ostp-prober`) that tries every carrier against a
  server and estimates where the filtering box is by TTL, but it's rough and
  prints a lot of noise; it needs work before its output is worth sharing.

### Questions

1. The MegaFon UDP case — a few hundred bytes back, then nothing. Does that match
   what others see from TSPU against fully encrypted UDP (the first packets pass,
   then the flow is cut)? Any idea what triggers it: entropy, packet sizes, the
   destination ASN?
2. For traffic carried inside TLS: what inner shaping is actually worth doing
   against encapsulated-handshake fingerprinting?
3. Decoy responses vs silent drop for unauthenticated probes — which one has
   held up better against TSPU's active probing in your experience?


All this message also written by Claude. Sorry about that.

issues.title: QUIC on 1280-byte IP paths: should initial packets start at 1200 bytes?
issues.body:
Should Yggdrasil start QUIC links with 1200-byte packets to support paths with IP MTU 1280, or should this remain entirely a quic-go fallback policy?

I reproduced a connection problem on `develop` at `2c7f050fc5398ecd8ac5f77e9bb5bd91aa2e9e35` (quic-go v0.64.1, Go 1.26.9). A proposed application-level change and regression test are available in [commit b37b195](https://github.com/krivonosoff161/yggdrasil-go/commit/b37b19588936020682f3c442c9d963d84211040b). I would like to confirm the intended behaviour and whether that change belongs here.

### Small reproducible example

Use the production QUIC link listener, dialler and TLS configuration, with a local UDP relay between them. The relay forwards datagrams in both directions but drops those exceeding the path's payload limit. It does not return a local send error or fabricate QUIC responses.

| Path | UDP payload limit | Current configuration | InitialPacketSize=1200 on both endpoints |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IPv4, IP MTU 1500 | 1472 bytes | connection and transfer pass | pass |
| IPv4, IP MTU 1280 | 1252 bytes | handshake timeout | 4096-byte request and reply pass |
| IPv6, IP MTU 1280 | 1232 bytes | handshake timeout | 4096-byte request and reply pass |

The [regression test](https://github.com/krivonosoff161/yggdrasil-go/blob/b37b19588936020682f3c442c9d963d84211040b/src/core/link_quic_test.go) is included in that commit. With the test added to the base code, the two low-MTU cases fail; with the three-line production change, all cases pass. Run it with:

```sh
go test -count=1 -v -run TestQUICLinkThroughLimitedPath ./src/core
```

The proposed change is in the shared listener/dialler configuration in `src/core/link_quic.go`:

```go
// Inside the existing quic.Config:
InitialPacketSize: 1200,
```

The default initial UDP payload is 1280 bytes, which becomes 1308 bytes with IPv4/UDP headers or 1328 with IPv6/UDP headers. If the smaller MTU is on an intermediate router, a local write can succeed while the packet is dropped further along the path. The local `EMSGSIZE` fallback added in quic-go 0.64 does not cover that silent-drop case. Path MTU discovery remains enabled with the proposed setting.

### Routed failure and recovery

I also tested actual Yggdrasil processes across two Linux kernel routers in isolated network namespaces:

1. Establish the QUIC link with path MTU 1500 and successfully request a roughly 12 KiB NodeInfo response.
2. Lower the intermediate link MTU to 1280 while keeping the endpoint links at 1500.
3. Request the same response again.

Before the change, the large request fails, the peer goes down, and no recovery is observed during 85 seconds at MTU 1280. Restoring MTU 1500 restores communication. With 1200 configured on both endpoints, the first large request still fails, but the following small and large requests succeed while the path remains at MTU 1280. This was observed both with ICMP fragmentation-needed messages delivered and with them blocked, with packet-header captures and router counters checked.

This does **not** establish that the change fixes every PMTU decrease on an existing connection. The initial failed request remains, mixed-version peers may still send larger initial packets, and throughput impact has not been benchmarked. The established-connection black-hole problem is already tracked in [quic-go#5914](https://github.com/quic-go/quic-go/issues/5914). Related work includes the merged [local-error fallback #5911](https://github.com/quic-go/quic-go/pull/5911) and closed [handshake retry proposal #5936](https://github.com/quic-go/quic-go/pull/5936); I am not proposing to duplicate that library work here.

Local validation: Windows full Go test suite and `go vet` pass; all seven Linux test-package binaries were executed successfully in an isolated network namespace, including IPv6. NAT state loss, translated-port change and conntrack expiry also recovered with the candidate. GitHub CI has not run.

issues.title: Link-quality telemetry: link RTT, loss and queue in getPeers (design proposal)
issues.body:
## Summary

`getPeers` exposes `latency` per peer. Operators read it as link latency; it is an EWMA of **router
signature-response** times refreshed every **4 minutes** (`ironwood/network/router.go:53`,
`network/config.go:26`, published in `src/admin/getpeers.go`). There is no link-level RTT, loss or
queue signal anywhere in the admin surface — per-peer **throughput** is covered since 0.5.15
(`rate_recvd`/`rate_sent`), latency is not.

Consequence: any adaptive decision (operator tooling, or the daemon itself) is made on data that is
minutes old and answers a different question than the one being asked.

## Measurements behind this (v0.5.15, real path)

| Measurement | Result |
|---|---|
| Overlay vs raw TCP over the same path | 87.2 vs 85.7 Mbit/s (noise) |
| Overlay RTT | 55.8 ms, same as the tunnel |
| Protocol overhead | 2.6% |
| TUN MTU 1420 instead of 65535 | −25% |
| 4 streams vs 1 | no gain (path-bound) |
| CPU at 87 Mbit/s | 16% of one core on the VPS |

The overlay is close to free; what is missing is per-peer degradation signal.

## Proposal (stage 1, additive and wire-compatible)

1. New link packet pair `wirePing`/`wirePong` (type byte + 8-byte nonce), every 10 s per peer with
   ±20% jitter, answered immediately; sent **only** when both sides advertise the new minor version.
2. Per-peer state: RTT (EWMA α=1/8), jitter, loss counters (sent/answered, monotonic), queue bytes.
   `pDelay` (`network/peers.go:123`) is declared but never updated — a natural home for this.
3. Additive `getPeers` fields: `link_rtt_ms`, `link_rtt_jitter_ms`, `link_loss_ppm`,
   `link_ping_age_s`, `queue_bytes`, and `latency_source: "router_ewma"` so the existing value stops
   being misread. Missing measurement is `null`, never zero.

Cost: 9 bytes per peer per 10 s each way, one timer per peer.

## Stage 2 (separate review)

Optional operator-visible scoring with hysteresis/dwell, and an off-by-default parent preference that
can only reorder existing valid candidates. No tree changes, no invented paths.

## Compatibility

Old peers never receive the new packet type; old consumers ignore additive JSON fields; routing and
config are unchanged in stage 1. A mixed-version pair exchanges traffic with zero pings.

## Acceptance criteria

1. `link_rtt` within ±2 ms of external ICMP p50 on the same path.
2. ≤2% throughput regression at 500 Mbit/s with 50 peers.
3. 5% `netem` loss shows `link_loss_ppm` within ±1%.
4. Mixed-version interop: zero ping packets, zero errors.
5. No timer/goroutine leak on disconnect.

## Out of scope

Padding, fixed cells and mixing delays — they change the wire format and the latency contract and
deserve their own RFC. This one is their prerequisite.

Full document (problem, alternatives, effort, reproduction steps): happy to attach or paste it here
on request. Stage 1 is ~300 lines plus tests; I can open it as a PR if this direction is acceptable.

issues.title: deb: keep configuration backups private
issues.body:
## Summary

On Debian package upgrades, `postinst` backs up the existing configuration under `/var/backups`. Older configurations can be mode 0644, so a plain copy leaves the backup containing the private key readable by other users. Create the backup through a mode 0600 temporary file and replace any existing dated backup atomically. The backup date is now determined when the package is installed.

This addresses the backup path described in #697. Permissions on the active configuration were fixed separately.

- [x] `sh -n contrib/deb/generate.sh` and `sh -n contrib/deb/test-postinst-backup.sh`
- [x] `sh contrib/deb/test-postinst-backup.sh` (regression fails on the previous backup implementation and passes with this change, including replacement of a mode 0644 backup)

issues.title: Add experimental Plan 9 / 9front support
issues.body:
## Summary

Adds the platform-specific layers to run yggdrasil as a **full node on Plan 9 (9front)**: a TUN adapter, link-local multicast peer discovery, and platform defaults. No changes to the supported-platform code paths — the shared multicast logic (`_announce`/`listen`/`_stop`) is byte-for-byte unchanged.

## What was verified

- **Builds**: `plan9/amd64`, `plan9/386`, `linux`, `darwin`, `freebsd`, `openbsd` all `go build` clean; `go vet` clean on plan9; `go test ./src/...` passes on linux (no regression).
- **Runtime on a real 9front grid**: the cross-compiled binary runs as a node — the `pkt` TUN interface comes up with the `0200::/7` address (MTU clamped to the medium's 4096), multicast beacons are sent and received via `/net/udp`, and peers connect **both inbound and outbound**. Graceful shutdown on the `interrupt` note unbinds the interface cleanly.

## Design

**TUN** (`src/tun/tun_plan9.go`): Plan 9 has no in-kernel TUN device. The equivalent is a `pkt` packet interface (`ipifc`) per `ip(3)` — `bind pkt`, `add` the `0200::/7` address, and read/write raw IPv6 through `/net/ipifc/N/data`. This is the same primitive `6in4(8)`/`ppp(8)` use. Implemented as a `wgtun.Device` so the existing TUN read/write goroutines work unchanged. On startup it reclaims any stale ipifc still carrying our address (Plan 9 doesn't reap a `pkt` ipifc when its owner is hard-killed, unlike a Linux tun).

**Multicast** (`src/multicast/multicast_plan9.go`): `golang.org/x/net/ipv6` is stubbed on Plan 9, so the beacon socket is driven natively through `/net/udp` in "headers" mode (`announce *!port`, `addmulti` to join `ff02::114`, 52-byte `Udphdr` with big-endian ports). To avoid touching the shared multicast code, `plan9Sock` mirrors the exact subset of `*ipv6.PacketConn` method signatures that `multicast.go` calls (`JoinGroup`/`WriteTo`/`ReadFrom`/`Close`); `ReadFrom` returns an `*ipv6.ControlMessage{Dst:…}` so the shared `listen()`'s existing `rcm.Dst` checks work as-is. Only the `Multicast` struct + `_start` (socket creation) are per-platform — the non-Plan-9 versions are moved **verbatim** to `multicast_sock.go`. Reclaims stale UDP convs on startup + retries `announce` to handle a port freed mid-shutdown.

## Caveats / notes

- **Admin socket**: listens on TCP loopback (`tcp://localhost:9001`) and requires a configured loopback interface (`ipconfig loopback /dev/null 127.1 /128`). The admin socket has no auth and relies on loopback binding for security, so it intentionally does not fall back to a wildcard bind. Documented in the README.
- **Hard shutdown**: a `slay`/crash leaves the `pkt` ipifc and `0200::/7` route behind; the next start reclaims them. A clean `interrupt`-note shutdown unbinds normally.
- `contrib/ansible/genkeys.go` is excluded from plan9 builds (the `cheggaaa/pb` `termutil.TerminalSize` symbol has no plan9 definition — appears to be an upstream `pb` bug worth filing separately).
- CI adds plan9/amd64 + plan9/386 **cross-compile** jobs (no plan9 test runner; tests can't run, only build-verified).
- Runtime-verified on 9front **amd64**; the 386 target compiles but wasn't run.

This is experimental and Plan 9 is a niche target that the maintainers can't easily test, so I'm happy to maintain this going forward and to open a tracking issue if useful. Feedback welcome — in particular on whether the `multicast_sock.go` split (moving the struct + `_start` out of `multicast.go`) is an acceptable way to branch the plan9 execution, or if you'd prefer a different structure.

issues.title: Design discussion: privacy and adaptive routing as the network grows
issues.body:
# Design discussion: privacy and adaptive routing as the network grows

Status: proposal for discussion · Date: 2026-10-25 · Companion to #1403

## 1. Premise

Yggdrasil is pleasant at 10³ nodes and will be asked to behave at 10⁵–10⁶. At that size two
properties stop being “nice to have”:

1. **Operators cannot see link quality** (one 4-minute router EWMA, no RTT/loss/queue), so every
   routing decision — human or automatic — is blind.
2. **Traffic metadata is fully visible to forwarding nodes** (`source`/`dest` public keys in the
   `traffic` struct), so “private network” means private from the outside, not from the path.

This document proposes a staged, opt-in answer to both, with costs measured on a real path
(v0.5.15, home host ↔ Hetzner VPS, 2026-10-24): overlay ≈ raw TCP (87.2 vs 85.7 Mbit/s), RTT
55.8 ms both, protocol overhead 2.6%, `IfMTU 1420` costs **−25%**, four parallel streams give no
gain (path-bound), CPU 16% of one core at 87 Mbit/s.

## 2. Part A — adaptive routing (measured, not guessed)

| Stage | Content | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | Link telemetry: per-peer RTT/jitter/loss/age, additive admin fields (#1403, code linked there) | low: off by default, no routing change |
| A2 | Peer scoring with **dwell (30 s)** and **hysteresis (20%)**, plus a disjoint-secondary rule; only reorders existing valid candidates | medium: behaviour, needs policy agreement |
| A3 | Optional multipath for bulk flows (reordering buffer, latency cost) | high: only if A1/A2 prove value |

Non-goals: replacing tree routing; per-packet re-routing in ironwood; promising bandwidth. At
10⁶ nodes the bottleneck for an individual is still their last mile — our four-stream test shows
routing cannot add capacity, only avoid a bad peer.

## 3. Part B — privacy (opt-in, priced)

Threat model first: hide *content and size/timing* from a path observer and from the last mile;
**not** hide that two nodes talk from a global observer, and not defend against an endpoint that
is compromised.

| Stage | Content | Cost (measured/modeled) |
|---|---|---|
| B1 | Posture and cost accounting in the console (`privacy`), disabled by default | zero |
| B2 | Fixed-size cells + Poisson release jitter for opted-in flows | +10–60% bandwidth depending on chunk size; +20–75 ms p95 |
| B3 | Cover traffic with a hard share budget (AGC-style), only with an economic story | ~82 kbit/s per node at 1 cell / 200 ms |
| B4 | Mixnet transport (external, e.g. Nym-style) for those who need unobservability | latency measured in hundreds of ms |

Key findings that shape the design:

- **Cell size is the expensive decision, not cryptography.** Overhead is set by the chunk
  distribution: with 2 KiB cells, 1280-byte writes cost +60%, aligned writes ~0. A single
  “typical” number would be dishonest, so the console computes it from a measured chunk size.
- **Smaller cells are not automatically cheaper**; fragmentation can beat padding (our calibration
  picks the cheapest cell within a budget, tie-broken towards fewer packets).
- **Anonymity is a crowd problem.** Below a minimum observed participant count the strongest
  profile is refused; the count is a local observation, labelled as such.
- **Privacy must not write logs.** An enabled posture cannot combine with per-flow logging; this
  is enforced in code, not documentation.
- **Padding must not break the path.** Forcing small MTU already costs 25%; profiles therefore pad
  logical cells, not the TUN MTU, and `bulk` keeps jumbo frames.

## 4. How A and B interact

- Path diversity helps both: fewer nodes see a full flow, and one bad peer cannot carry everything.
- Padding and jitter cost the same resources routing wants (bandwidth, latency), so both are
  opt-in and priced before enabling.
- If privacy is on and the path degrades, the *honest* behaviour is to say so, not to silently
  disable privacy to keep a number green.

## 5. Compatibility and rollout

- A1/B1 are additive and off by default; A2/B2 need explicit opt-in and

issues.title: SIGSEGV in DSASigner::Sign when OpenSSL provider refuses DSA signing
issues.body:
i2pd crashes with a SIGSEGV in DSASigner::Sign (libi2pd/Signature.cpp, around line 86) on systems where OpenSSL refuses DSA operations, and the crash is fully reproducible on demand. The root cause is that the return values of EVP_DigestSignInit and EVP_DigestSign are never checked, so when the provider key management refuses the DSA key, the signing call fails silently and leaves the output buffer full of garbage. The subsequent d2i_DSA_SIG then returns NULL on that invalid data, and the NULL pointer goes straight into DSA_SIG_get0, which dereferences it and takes the process down.

I'm hitting this on i2pd 2.59.0 running on Fedora 44/rawhide, with update-crypto-policies --show reporting DEFAULT. On this system even openssl genpkey -algorithm DSA fails outright with "provider keymgmt failure", so DSA simply cannot be assumed to work at all here. Any distro or setup where the OpenSSL provider refuses DSA should behave the same way.

The crash is remotely reachable through SAM. Opening a SAM connection and sending SESSION CREATE with STYLE=STREAM and DESTINATION=TRANSIENT, omitting SIGNATURE_TYPE, gives the session SIGNING_KEY_TYPE_DSA_SHA1 by default (SAMBridge::CreateSession in SAM.cpp), and the router dies the moment the transient destination tries to sign its first LeaseSet. Since anyone able to reach the SAM port can trigger this, it feels more serious than an ordinary local crash.

The failing path looks like this: EVP_DigestSignInit(ctx, NULL, EVP_sha1(), NULL, m_PrivateKey) followed by EVP_DigestSign(ctx, sign, &l, buf, len) with the result ignored, then DSA_SIG *sig = d2i_DSA_SIG(NULL, &s1, l) yielding NULL on failure, and finally DSA_SIG_get0(sig, &r, &s) where the segfault happens. Backtrace of the crashing thread:

```
#0  DSA_SIG_get0 (sig=0x0, ...) at crypto/dsa/dsa_sign.c:137
#1  i2p::crypto::DSASigner::Sign (...) at libi2pd/Signature.cpp:86
#2  i2p::data::PrivateKeys::Sign (...) at libi2pd/Identity.cpp:658
#3  i2p::data::LocalLeaseSet2::LocalLeaseSet2 (...) at libi2pd/LeaseSet.cpp:948
...
#11 i2p::client::ClientDestination::CreateNewLeaseSet (...) at libi2pd/Destination.cpp:1497
#12 i2p::client::LeaseSetDestination::UpdateLeaseSet (...) at libi2pd/Destination.cpp:272
```

As a fix, the signer should at minimum validate the EVP calls and fail cleanly instead of dereferencing NULL. It might also be worth considering a fallback to a signature type the local OpenSSL actually supports, since DSA can no longer be taken for granted. Related to this, when CreateSession receives a SIGNATURE_TYPE that fails to resolve it currently just logs a warning and keeps going with the DSA default, which I would expect to be a hard error at session creation time rather than a deferred crash. Happy to attach the full backtrace and core dump if useful.

issues.title: Check read and write results for torrent files and reopen a broken stream
issues.body:
As asked in #dev by orignal and R4SAS.

`TorrentFile::Save` and `Load` did not look at the result of the write or the read, so a failed write was reported as success. Worse, the failure leaves the error flag set on the stream while the file stays open, and `Open` only opens when the file is closed - so every later call failed silently for the life of the object, while `m_LastAccessTime` kept being updated so the file was not closed by inactivity either.

Now both calls check the stream after the operation, log the error with `strerror` and return false, and `Open` closes and clears a stream that is open but in a failed state before reopening it. The periodic flush is checked too, since that is where a buffered write actually reaches the disk.

Measured with a harness that sets `RLIMIT_FSIZE` to 64 KB and writes past it:

| step | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| write at offset 0 | true | true |
| write past the size limit | true | true (buffered, see below) |
| write at offset 2048 after the failure | true (nothing written) | false |
| read at offset 0 | false | true |

The file on disk holds 1024 bytes in both cases - that is, the second and third writes were lost while reporting success. After the change the lost write is reported, and the stream recovers for the next call instead of staying broken.

One honest limitation: writes are buffered, so a write that oversteps a limit still returns true at that moment and the error surfaces on the next call or on the flush. Forcing a flush per block would make it immediate, but that is a different trade-off on disk IO, so I left it to you. Build without warnings, unit tests pass.

issues.title: Check stream errors when verifying SU3 signature
issues.body:
As pointed out in #dev: the SU3 signature verification does not look at stream errors.

Two things in that block. The stream position was taken into a `size_t`, and `tellg` returns -1 on a stream error, which turns into a huge value and then into `tbsLen` and `new uint8_t[tbsLen]`. And the results of the two reads were not checked at all: on a truncated file the digest is computed over the whole declared length, with everything past what was read being uninitialized memory from `new`.

Now the position is checked for a negative value, and each read is checked against the length it was supposed to deliver, with the buffers freed before returning.

Measured with a harness that feeds a file whose declared content length is 64 MB while the file itself is 121 bytes, with a signer whose certificate is present (otherwise the branch is never reached): before the change the log says only "SU3 signature verification failed" - that is, the incomplete data was hashed as if it were whole and the blame fell on the signature; after it the log says "SU3 signed data is incomplete: 121 of 67108921" and parsing stops there. Both return 0, so nothing else changes for the caller. Build without warnings, unit tests pass.

issues.title: REALITY: authenticated handshake fails with `padding: -4` when the target sends an empty EncryptedExtensions (since v26.10.21)
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

Since v26.10.21 (REALITY `83f621788ca8`), every authenticated REALITY connection fails when the target sends an **empty EncryptedExtensions** (no SNI ack, no ALPN, nothing else). With `"show": true` the server prints:

```
hs.handshake() err: payload[0]: 8, padding: -4
```

v26.9.9 (REALITY `8cdf7bf9c7f0`) works with the same target.

Cause:

- XTLS/REALITY `3c98159` ("Sync upstream Go 1.27+", #30) added to `handshake_server_tls13.go`:
  ```go
  if !hs.c.didResume && hs.clientHello.serverName != "" {
      encryptedExtensions.serverNameAck = true
  }
  ```
  An authenticated connection always carries SNI unless `serverNames` contains `""`, so REALITY's own EncryptedExtensions now always has the 4-byte empty `server_name` extension. Before this commit `encryptedExtensionsMsg` had no such field.
- `[REALITY] SECTION: mimic recorded handshakeLen` in `conn.go` pads each handshake record to the length recorded from the target and returns `payload[0]: %v, padding: %v` when its own record is longer (`payload[0]: 8` is EncryptedExtensions).
- REALITY's own EncryptedExtensions has no ALPN, so it is now 4 bytes longer than an empty one. A target whose EncryptedExtensions is empty gives a 28-byte record (including the 5-byte record header) against REALITY's 32, hence padding -4. Any extension on the target side (an SNI ack, ALPN, ...) is at least 4 bytes and absorbs it.

Not setting `serverNameAck` in the REALITY server (the pre-sync behaviour) looks sufficient, since padding then matches any target; I have not tested a patch.

This is easy to miss: the fallback path does not reach this code, so probing the node without the key looks fine, and without `show` the server logs only an Info line (`REALITY: processed invalid connection ...: handshake did not complete successfully`) while the client gets EOF. We hit it on a production node whose target neither acks SNI nor negotiates ALPN. To check a target, look for any extension besides `supported versions` and `key share`:

```
openssl s_client -connect <Domain>:443 -servername <Domain> -tls1_3 -alpn h2,http/1.1 -tlsextdebug </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep 'TLS server extension'
```

### Reproduction Method

All on loopback (Linux, OpenSSL 3.5.5). Three `openssl s_server` targets with the same self-signed certificate for `example.test`:

```
openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -keyout k.pem -out c.pem -days 30 -subj /CN=example.test -addext subjectAltName=DNS:example.test
# A: empty EncryptedExtensions
openssl s_server -accept 127.0.0.1:20443 -cert c.pem -key k.pem -tls1_3 -www -quiet
# B: acks SNI (s_server acks only when -servername installs its callback and the name matches)
openssl s_server -accept 127.0.0.1:20444 -cert c.pem -key k.pem -tls1_3 -www -quiet -servername example.test -cert2 c.pem -key2 k.pem
# C: no SNI ack, but negotiates ALPN
openssl s_server -accept 127.0.0.1:20445 -cert c.pem -key k.pem -tls1_3 -www -quiet -alpn h2,http/1.1
# something to fetch through the proxy
python3 -m http.server 18080 --bind 127.0.0.1
```

Start the server (config below, `target` pointing at A, B or C) and the client (always v26.10.21), then `curl -x socks5h://127.0.0.1:11080 http://127.0.0.1:18080/`:

| server | target | target EE record | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| v26.10.21 | A | 28 | curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer; `padding: -4` |
| v26.10.21 | B | 32 | 200 |

Direct/Freedom outbound: Close blocked connections after `blockDelay` (VLESS, Hysteria, etc.)
issues.body:
Regression from #6060 (958eb9e). `blackhole` waits for `buf.Copy(input, buf.Discard)` and relies on the `blockDelay` timer calling `common.Interrupt(input)` to end it. That only works for a pipe: VLESS, Hysteria and other inbounds that use `DispatchLink` pass a reader on the client connection, and `Interrupt` does nothing to it. So a blocked connection stays open until the client closes it, whatever `blockDelay` is. In our tests it was still open after 330 s, longer than `connIdle`.

Drain the input in a goroutine and return once the delay has passed or the input has ended. The inbound then closes the connection, as it does after the blackhole outbound.

`TestVlessBlockDelay` covers `blockDelay` 0 and 1 through a VLESS inbound. Both cases fail on main.

issues.title: grpc: close cached clients with their outbound handler
issues.body:
Related to #7177. Requesting review of resource ownership, shutdown semantics, and API compatibility

## Problem

Outbound gRPC clients are cached by destination and MemoryStreamConfig, but core shutdown never closes or removes them. In an embedding process that stays alive, clients can retain connections and continue reconnecting after their core has stopped.

## Change

Give memory stream settings synchronous close-hook registration, and close the resources from their owning outbound handler. Register each ClientConn for exact-entry cache removal and ClientConn.Close. Refuse both reuse and creation after owner closure starts; racing creation must either register for cleanup or close its unpublished client. Cleanup runs outside the settings/cache locks, and concurrent Close callers wait for the same result.

The supported Instance lifecycle is single-start. Each fresh core retains separate ownership even when endpoint and outbound tags match. No per-run generation model, idle-timeout change or per-RPC closure of the shared ClientConn is added.

## Validation

- Synthetic regression reproduces the problem on v26.3.27 and main da2248c.
- `go test -race ./transport/internet ./transport/internet/grpc -count=1 -timeout=120s` passes on this exact branch.
- Official `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./` passes.
- Tests cover two live cores, sibling streams, normal/MultiMode, fresh-core cycles, failed-start cleanup, multiple destinations, owner/acquisition races, cancellation/backoff and forced dialerProxy lookup contention with Manager.Close.
- Earlier candidate testing also ran the target race suites five times and the dialerProxy test ten times. Those results are supplementary, not a claim that the whole upstream suite passes.

## Review questions / limits

- Handler.Close previously always returned nil. This candidate propagates cleanup errors. Is propagation preferred, or should transport cleanup be logged while preserving the existing return policy? Embedders must distinguish a cleanup error from a still-running core.
- MemoryStreamConfig with resource/mutex state must not be copied; direct external transport callers must close their settings.
- Manager.RemoveHandler still bypasses Handler.Close. XHTTP/nested download settings and TUN eventfd cleanup remain unfixed.
- No general multi-instance guarantee for Xray's other process-global networking state, TLS/Reality/masking matrix, or physical Android packet boundary is claimed.

This is intended as a draft for ownership/API review, not a claim that the Android product defect is resolved.

### 描述

在 Windows 11 上使用 Xray-core 连接 VLESS + REALITY + Vision 节点时，发现 TCP 下载吞吐量在部分网络条件下明显低于 Linux 和 Android。

本地宽带约为 100 Mbps。在网络条件较差、可能存在拥堵或丢包的时段，Windows 原生 Xray 的下载速度通常只有 10～30 Mbps，最近一次测试甚至只有约 10 Mbps。

但在同一时段：

- Android v2rayNG 连接同一节点，可以达到约 90 Mbps。
- 同一台 Windows 电脑通过 WSL2 Linux 运行相同版本的 Xray-core，可以达到约 90 Mbps。
- 在 Windows 原生 Xray 的 TCP 出站中显式设置 `SO_RCVBUF = 2 MiB` 后，下载速度可以从约 10 Mbps 提升至约 85 Mbps。

Windows 和 WSL2 Linux 使用完全相同的 Xray-core 版本。

因此，这个问题并不依赖于 v2rayN 的运行逻辑，更可能与 Windows 原生 Xray 建立的 TCP 连接、Socket 缓冲区行为或 Go/Windows 网络实现有关。

不过，目前还无法确定根本原因属于 Xray-core、Go 运行时还是 Windows TCP 协议栈。

#### 测试环境

| 项目 | 信息 |
|---|---|
| Windows 系统 | Windows 11 26H2 |
| Windows OS Build | 26300.9711 |
| Windows 运行方式 | 命令行直接运行 `xray.exe`，不使用图形客户端 |
| Windows Xray-core | v26.10.21 |
| WSL2 Linux Xray-core | v26.10.21 |
| Android 客户端 | v2rayNG 2.3.13 (xray v26.10.21) |
| 协议 | VLESS |
| 传输 | TCP |
| 安全协议 | REALITY |
| Flow | xtls-rprx-vision |
| VPS TCP 拥塞控制 | BBR |
| RTT | 约 140～180 ms |
| 本地宽带 | 约 100 Mbps |

Mux 和 Fragment 均未启用。

此前分别使用有线以太网和 Wi-Fi 测试，均出现过相同问题。

#### 最新的同一时段对照测试

在网络条件较差的同一时段，使用相同 Reality 节点进行了以下测试：

| 测试方式 | 下载速度 |
|---|---|
| Android v2rayNG | 约 90 Mbps |
| Windows 原生 Xray，默认 Socket 配置 | 约 10 Mbps |
| Windows 原生 Xray，设置 `SO_RCVBUF = 2 MiB` | 约 85 Mbps |
| WSL2 Linux Xray，相同核心版本 | 约 90 Mbps |


两次测试使用相同的 Reality 节点和相同的出站配置，主要变化是 TCP Socket 的 `SO_RCVBUF` 设置。

在相近的网络条件下，添加该设置后，Windows Xray 下载速度从约 10 Mbps 提升到了约 85 Mbps。

此前还尝试将 `SO_RCVBUF` 从 2 MiB 增加到 4 MiB，但没有观察到明显的额外性能提升。

#### Windows 电脑通过 Android 代理的交叉验证

此前还进行了另一组测试：

让 Android v2rayNG 建立 Reality 出站连接，并在 Android 上提供 SOCKS5 代理。

同一台 Windows 电脑上的浏览器及 `curl` 通过该 SOCKS5 代理下载，可以达到接近 90～100 Mbps 的速度。

例如，下载相同的 Cloudflare 测试文件时，曾观察到：

- Windows 原生 Xray：约 2 MB/s。
- Windows 通过 Android 的 SOCKS5 代理：约 12 MB/s。

因此，Windows 浏览器、下载工具以及电脑本身的网络接入能力，并不能解释吞吐量差距。

#### 问题与网络条件有关

这个问题并不是全天持续存在。

在深夜网络条件较好时，即使完全删除 `SO_RCVBUF` 自定义设置，Windows 原生 Xray 也能够达到约 85～90 Mbps。

因此，这不是 Windows Xray 始终被限制在 10～30 Mbps 的固定性能瓶颈。

更准确地说：

**在某些网络条件下，Windows 原生 Xray 的 TCP 吞吐量明显低于 Linux/Android，而显式设置较大的 SO_RCVBUF 后，性能下降得到显著缓解。**

#### VPS 端的 TCP 状态观察

此前在 VPS 上使用以下命令观察测速期间的 TCP 状态：

```bash
ss -tin state established '( sport = :443 )'
```

发现以下现象：

**Windows 原生 Xray 下载速度较低时：**

- 部分主要数据连接的 `snd_wnd` 约为 128～256 KiB。
- 部分连接存在一定比例的 `rwnd_limited` 时间。
- 能观察到 TCP 重传、乱序等现象。

**Android v2rayNG 下载速度正常时：**

- 部分主要数据连接的 `snd_wnd` 可以达到约 4 MiB。
- 同样存在 TCP 重传，部分连接的重传字节数并不少。
- 尽管存在重传，仍然能够保持较高下载吞吐量。

#### 已尝试的排查

1. **排除图形客户端影响**

   Windows 测试直接运行 `xray.exe`，不用 v2rayN。

2. **排除 Xray-core 版本差异**

   Windows 原生 Xray 和 WSL2 Linux Xray 使用完全相同的 v26.10.21。

   在相同时段，Linux 版能够达到约 90 Mbps，而 Windows 默认 Socket 配置只有约 10 Mbps。

3. **排除浏览器及下载工具**

   使用不同浏览器代理方式和 `curl --socks5-hostname` 测试，均观察到原生 Windows Xray 速度偏低。

4. **排除网卡连接方式**

   Windows 使用有线以太网和 Wi-Fi 均曾复现问题。

5. **Windows TCP 自动调优**

   Windows TCP 接收窗口自动调优原本为 `Normal`。

   曾临时修改为 `Experimental`，没有明显改善，之后已经恢复 `Normal`。

6. **测试 VPS 拥塞控制**

   VPS 原本使用 BBR。

   曾临时切换至 CUBIC，Windows 下载速度反而进一步下降至个位数 Mbps，随后恢复 BBR。

7. **测试更大的 SO_RCVBUF**

   设置 2 MiB 后，Windows 吞吐量明显改善。

   进一步增加至 4 MiB，没有观察到明显的额外提升。

### 重现方式

**前提：**

该问题在本人网络条件较差的时段更容易复现。网络状况良好时，默认配置也可能达到满速。

**1. 使用默认 Socket 配置运行 Windows Xray**

Windows 系统：

```

通过本地 SOCKS5 代理进行下载测速。

在问题出现时，下载速度约为 10～30 Mbps，最近一次测试约为 10 Mbps。

issues.title: Windows: core fails to start with 'The system cannot find the path specified' when the working directory contains a directory junction (regression in v26.10.21)
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

On Windows, Xray fails to start when the **current working directory** contains a directory junction:

```
Failed to start: main: failed to load config files: [config.json] > infra/conf/serial: failed to read config: &{Name:config.json Format:json} > The system cannot find the path specified.
```

The config file itself exists and is readable — the failure happens while Xray resolves the path of an already opened file.

### Versions

- Xray core **v26.10.21** (go1.27.3 windows/amd64) — broken
- Xray core **v26.9.30** — works (the code path described below does not exist there)

### Steps to reproduce

```bat
mkdir C:\test\target
echo {}> C:\test\target\config.json
mklink /J C:\test\link C:\test\target

cd /d C:\test\link
xray run -c config.json
```

Result:

```
Xray 26.10.21 (Xray, Penetrates Everything.) 1b1647c (go1.27.3 windows/amd64)
[Info] infra/conf/serial: Reading config: &{Name:config.json Format:json}
Failed to start: main: failed to load config files: [config.json] > infra/conf/serial: failed to read config: &{Name:config.json Format:json} > The system cannot find the path specified.
```

With the **physical** path it works:

```bat
cd /d C:\test\target
xray run -c config.json
[Info] infra/conf/serial: Reading config: &{Name:config.json Format:json}
[Warning] core: Xray 26.10.21 started
```

### Root cause

`main/confloader/external/external.go`, function `readConfigFile()` (introduced in v26.10.21):

```go
path, err := filepath.Abs(file.Name())
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
path, err = filepath.EvalSymlinks(path)
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
switch strings.ToLower(filepath.Ext(path)) {
case ".jsonc", ".json", ".yml", ".yaml", ".toml", ".pb", ".protobuf":
default:
    return nil, errors.New("unsupported config file extension: ", path)
}
```

`filepath.EvalSymlinks` fails on Windows with `ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND` ("The system cannot find the path specified") as soon as one component of the path is a **directory junction** (this is a Go standard library behavior, see the related golang/go report).

Notes:
- the file has already been opened successfully at this point (`os.Open(arg)` succeeded);
- the resolved path is only used for an **extension whitelist** check, so the resolution itself is not required;
- the failure is fatal and prevents the core from starting at all.

### Impact

Every user whose Xray is launched with a working directory located under a junction / symlinked directory is affected, e.g.:

- Scoop: `C:\Users\<user>\scoop\apps\<app>\current` is a junction to the versioned folder;
- Chocolatey / WinGet shim directories;
- any manually created `mklink /J` layout.

This is not only a CLI issue: for example **v2rayN** (which starts the core with `run -c config.json` and `WorkingDirectory = <install dir>\binConfigs`) becomes completely unusable after updating the bundled core to v26.10.21 — the client shows `Failed to start: main: failed to load config files: [config.json] ... The system cannot find the path specified.` and no proxy is available.

### Suggested fix

Do not let the symlink resolution failure be fatal — fall back to the unresolved path and check the extension with `filepath.Ext`:

```go
path, err := filepath.Abs(file.Name())
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
if resolved, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(path); err == nil {
    path = resolved
}
switch strings.ToLower(filepath.Ext(path)) {
case ".jsonc", ".json", ".yml", ".yaml", ".toml", ".pb", ".protobuf":
default:
    return nil, errors.New("unsupported config file extension: ", path)
}
```

### Minimal Go reproducer for the underlying behavior

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
)

func main() {
	p, err := filepath.Abs(os.Args[1])
	fmt.Println("Abs:         ", p, err)
	r, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(p)
	fmt.Println("EvalSymlinks:", r, err)
}
```

Run it with the CWD set to a junction directory and pass a file name inside it:

```bat
cd /d C:\test\link
go run main.go config.json
`

issues.title: Transport: Bind the UDP outbound socket with udp4/udp6 on OpenBSD
issues.body:
Follow-up to #6688.

#6688 binds the wildcard of the destination's family, but the merged version still passes the generic `"udp"` network to `ListenPacket`. For `"[::]:0"` Go also tries `0.0.0.0` (a lone `::` gets `IPv4zero` appended, golang/go#18806) and `ListenPacket` takes the first IPv4 address of the list. Where IPv4-mapped addresses exist that is still a dual-stack socket, so nothing shows up there. OpenBSD has no mapping: the socket stays `AF_INET` and every send to an IPv6 peer fails:

```
write udp 0.0.0.0:15085->[2001:4860:4806::]:123: address 2001:4860:4806::: non-IPv4 address
```

On v26.10.21 this broke IPv6 UDP (QUIC, DNS, NTP) through `freedom` on an OpenBSD transparent-proxy router: 208 such errors in the first ~90 minutes after the upgrade. The build I tested #6624/#6688 with passed `udp4`/`udp6` explicitly, which is why it did not show up in my testing.

This names the family explicitly on OpenBSD only: `udp4` for a v4 bind address, `udp6` for a v6 one (a `sendThrough` address goes through the same check). Other platforms keep the network string and the dual-stack socket they get today.

`TestDialUDPToIPv6` dials `[::1]` with `DialSystem` and writes one datagram. On OpenBSD 7.8 amd64 it fails without the change (`non-IPv4 address`) and passes with it; elsewhere it passes either way. The patched v26.10.21 has been running on the router since, and IPv6 UDP goes out from `[::]` again.

issues.title: [Feature request] XHTTP: optional idle filler on the download stream, so an idle connection survives a CDN's origin-silence timeout
issues.body:
### What happens

Behind Cloudflare (proxied record, any non-Enterprise plan), an XHTTP connection that carries no data for about two
minutes is closed by the CDN, and the proxied TCP connection inside it breaks. Long-lived but mostly silent
connections (chat and push sockets, SSH sessions, database connections) get torn down and rebuilt every couple of
minutes.

The same idle connection over WebSocket with `heartbeatPeriod` set survives, because the ping's pong is traffic
from the origin.

### Setup

- Server: VLESS + XHTTP (`mode: packet-up`), TLS, behind Cloudflare. Xray-core v26.x; the code path below is the
  same on `main`.
- Client: Xray-core v26.9.9, `alpn` h2 or h3, default xmux plus `hKeepAlivePeriod: 10`.

### Reproduce

1. Through the tunnel, open a TCP connection to an SSH server and log in, running a command that prints nothing for
   a while, e.g. `ssh -o ServerAliveInterval=0 -o TCPKeepAlive=no host 'sleep 200; echo done'`.
2. Silent for 110 s: `done` arrives. Silent for 200 s: the session dies at 125-128 s (`client_loop: send
   disconnect: Broken pipe`). Seen in every run.
3. Control: the same session through a WebSocket transport on a different CDN held 290 s silent with TCP
   keepalive off, at the default, and at 15 s, so the drop is specific to the XHTTP download path behind this CDN.

TCP keepalive (`sockopt.tcpKeepAliveIdle`) and `xmux.hKeepAlivePeriod` do not help: both end at the CDN edge, and
Cloudflare's timer counts silence from the origin. Cloudflare documents a 100 s limit for the origin's response
(error 524), and it can only be raised on Enterprise. The ~125 s drop observed mid-stream matches reports of
streaming responses behind Cloudflare.

### Why

In `transport/internet/splithttp/hub.go`, the stream-up upload POST gets a periodic filler in its response
(`scStreamUpServerSecs`, the goroutine that writes `X` padding), which keeps that request alive behind a CDN. The
download (`GET`, stream-down / packet-up, and stream-one) gets nothing while idle: after the headers and the first
flush, the server writes only real payload.

### Request

An option, off by default, for the server to put a filler on the download stream every N seconds while it is
idle (e.g. `scStreamDownServerSecs: "20-80"`, mirroring `scStreamUpServerSecs`), which the client discards. Since
the download body is not framed today, this probably needs a client that understands the filler, gated on the
version both sides already exchange (`x_version`) so older clients are never sent it.

An alternative that needs no new framing would also do: the client opening a fresh download request before the
current one has been idle for N seconds, handing the session over without losing data.

Happy to test a build.

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable error responses
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `errorResponse` object to the XHTTP inbound settings, replacing the bare status-only rejections with a service-consistent appearance.

Currently every rejected request is answered with a bare status code: no body, no `Content-Type` (Go's default "404 page not found" or nothing at all). From the terminating side (CDN, reverse proxy, monitoring) a server that answers *every* unknown path with a naked status code and no content type does not look like a normal service.

- `body` and `contentType` apply to every error response the hub writes (404 unknown path, 400/405/409/413/500 etc.), giving all rejections a uniform, service-consistent appearance.
- `statusCode` overrides the status for requests failing the padding validation — the effective authentication gate — allowing 403 semantics instead of the default 400.
- When `errorResponse` is unset, the behavior is unchanged.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "errorResponse": {
    "statusCode": 403,
    "body": "{\"error\":\"forbidden\"}",
    "contentType": "application/json"
  }
}
```

Resulting surface: unknown paths → `404 {"error":"forbidden"}`, the API gate without valid padding → `403` with the same body — a coherent API host instead of a bare 404/400 machine.

## Notes

- Server-side only. Round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 (matches all existing `.pb.go` headers; unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain).
- Proto field `errorResponse = 31` — merges cleanly alongside #7247 (`responseHeaders = 30`); both features are independent.

## Tests

- `Test_WriteErrorResponse`: bare default when unset, configured body + content type, padding-reject status default (400) and override (403).
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable response headers
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `responseHeaders` map (`map<string, string>`) to the XHTTP inbound settings, giving the server control over the headers it writes on responses.

Currently the hub hardcodes a set of response headers: the CORS block for the browser dialer (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`), `X-Accel-Buffering`, `Cache-Control` and the SSE `Content-Type`. With `responseHeaders` an operator can add, override, or remove any of them, as well as set arbitrary extra response headers.

## Semantics

- A key that doesn't collide with a default header is added to every response.
- A key that matches a hardcoded header overrides it.
- An empty value removes that header from the response entirely (including the hardcoded ones).
- When `responseHeaders` is unset, the behavior is byte-identical to before.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "responseHeaders": {
    "Server": "nginx",
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://example.com",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": ""
  }
}
```

## Why

- The CORS headers only matter for the browser dialer; a plain server deployment currently emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response, which is undesirable behind a specific origin and gets flagged by security reviews.
- Reverse-proxy and CDN setups sometimes require specific response headers (`Server`, `Via`, custom headers) or different cache semantics.
- Operators running behind intermediaries may want the response header set to stay consistent with the profile of the service they front, instead of carrying markers that no other service on that endpoint emits.

## Notes

- Server-side only; the client ignores it. It round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 — the header matches all existing `.pb.go` files (`check-proto` passes; I verified the unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain first).

## Tests

- `Test_SetResponseHeader`: default / override / removal via empty value.
- `Test_WriteResponseHeader_ResponseHeaders`: CORS default, override, removal, custom header addition, origin echo.
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: Sniffer: Don't count reads without new data as attempts
issues.body:
## Problem

TLS sniffing on a VLESS + Vision server almost always fails when the traffic comes through another Xray server with VLESS + Vision (a proxy chain). `routeOnly` gets no domain, and the connection is routed by IP only.

```
client → server 1 → server 2 → internet
```

All hops use VLESS + REALITY + `xtls-rprx-vision`. Server 2 has sniffing on the inbound and domain rules above an IP rule:

```json
"sniffing": { "enabled": true, "destOverride": ["http", "tls", "quic"], "routeOnly": true }
```
```json
{ "domain": ["geosite:habr"], "outboundTag": "direct-out" },
{ "ip": ["geoip:ru"], "outboundTag": "block-out" }
```

Opening https://habr.com in Chrome is blocked by the `geoip:ru` rule. The server 2 log has no `sniffed domain:` line for any `:443` connection, and the routing decision is made in under a millisecond, without waiting for the 200 ms sniffing deadline:

```
proxy/vless/inbound: firstLen = 1186
proxy/vless/inbound: received request for tcp:178.248.237.68:443
from 0.0.0.0:0 accepted tcp:178.248.237.68:443 [vless-tcp-reality-os-in -> block-out]
app/dispatcher: taking detour [block-out] for [tcp:178.248.237.68:443]
```

When the client connects to server 2 directly, the domain is sniffed.

## Root cause

1. **TLS record size.** `crypto/tls`, uTLS and REALITY use dynamic record sizing: for the first 128 KB of a connection a record is limited to `tcpMSSEstimate = 1208` bytes. In TLS 1.3 that leaves 1208 − 5 (record header) − 16 (AEAD tag) − 1 (inner content type) = **1186 bytes** of plaintext per record, which is the `firstLen = 1186` above.
2. **Client → server 1.** The client sends the whole ClientHello (~1.7–2 KB with `X25519MLKEM768`) as one Vision frame. The first record carries 44 bytes of VLESS request header, 21 bytes of Vision frame header and the first 1121 bytes of the ClientHello; the second record carries the rest of it plus padding. Server 1 reads the ClientHello as two chunks: 1121 bytes and the remainder.
3. **Server 1 → server 2.** The VLESS outbound on server 1 writes each chunk as a separate Vision frame with its own padding. For the first frame, 44 + 21 + 1121 = 1186 bytes fill the first record exactly, so the frame's padding goes into a record of its own. With the default testseed `{900, 500, 900, 256}`, content of 900 bytes or more gets 0–255 bytes of padding, so this happens unless the padding is 0, i.e. in about 255 of 256 connections.
4. **VisionReader on server 2.** For the padding-only record, [`VisionReader.ReadMultiBuffer`](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/1b1647cd9ddf0abc34b981d4611fc03bcac1ca74/proxy/proxy.go#L235-L243) strips the padding and returns an empty `MultiBuffer` with a nil error.
5. **Sniffer.** `cachedReader.Cache` gets no new data, but the [sniffing loop](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/1b1647cd9ddf0abc34b981d4611fc03bcac1ca74/app/dispatcher/default.go#L392-L421) runs the sniffers again on the same 1121 bytes. `SniffTLS` returns `ErrNoClue` again, because the TLS record is still incomplete, and the second `ErrNoClue` ends sniffing with `errSniffingTimeout`. The rest of the ClientHello arrives with the next read, too late.

Without server 1 there is no padding-only record between the two parts of the ClientHello, so two reads are enough.

## Reproduction

The chain was reproduced on one machine:

- Everything runs in an unprivileged network namespace (`unshare -rn`) with loopback MTU 1500.
- A local HTTPS server plays both `habr.com` and the REALITY target.
- **Client:** SOCKS inbound with sniffing and `routeOnly`, VLESS + REALITY + Vision outbound to server 1, or directly to server 2.
- **Server 1:** VLESS + REALITY + Vision inbound without sniffing, VLESS + REALITY + Vision outbound to server 2.
- **Server 2:** VLESS + REALITY + Vision inbound with sniffing and `routeOnly`. `domain:habr.com` goes to `freedom`, redirected to the local server; `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0` go to `blackhole`.
- **ClientHello sources:**
  - Headless Chrome 156 through `socks4://`, so t

issues.title: VLESS inbound: Close a removed user's live connections
issues.body:
RemoveUser only dropped the user from the validator, so connections that had already authenticated kept relaying until idle timeout, and Mux sub-connections reused them indefinitely. A panel enforcing a traffic or expiry limit through the API therefore had to restart the whole core to actually stop the user.

The inbound now tracks each authenticated connection under its exact MemoryUser and RemoveUser closes them; other users and a re-added user with the same email are unaffected. A connection that authenticates while the user is being removed re-checks the validator after registering, so it cannot slip past closeAll.

issues.title: DNS: honor nameserver timeouts for coalesced lookups
issues.body:
**Revised implementation:** [6ecd2853](https://github.com/eliotcougar/Xray-core/commit/6ecd2853f4af823312461b673ac733df21ad9754) · [complete focused diff against v26.10.21](https://github.com/eliotcougar/Xray-core/compare/1b1647cd9ddf0abc34b981d4611fc03bcac1ca74...6ecd2853f4af823312461b673ac733df21ad9754).

This PR was closed before the revised commits were pushed. Its Files changed view still shows the original head; the comparison above contains the implementation described here.

### Problem and practical effect

A foreground lookup can wait beyond its configured nameserver timeout when it joins an existing lookup for the same name and address family. In particular, an optimistic-cache refresh has an eight-second lifetime, while a foreground lookup may have a much shorter timeout. Blocking in `singleflight.Group.Do` delays returning to resolver selection and trying a healthy fallback.

The fix gives each waiter its own waiting lifetime and separates that from ownership of the shared operation. A short-lived waiter can leave promptly, while work needed by another waiter continues. It also prevents an earlier request's timeout from cancelling a shared query needed by a later request whose budget remains.

This is a nameserver-timeout correctness fix. The stable `LookupIP` interface remains context-free: closing an application connection does not automatically cancel its native DNS lookup. System-resolver cancellation is unchanged. No bulk-throughput or CPU improvement is claimed.

### Implementation

- Share queries per nameserver, domain and address family, with independent waiter contexts.
- Give the shared operation a bounded lifetime independent of the first waiter's deadline: eight seconds, extended for an explicitly longer nameserver timeout. Preserve routing context values.
- Cancel the operation when its last waiter leaves or DNS closes. A background refresh remains a waiter, retaining its existing eight-second policy.
- Handle A and AAAA independently, retaining a completed family when the other times out.
- Interrupt an owned TCP DNS connection on cancellation.
- Preserve single-family response TTLs and existing dual-stack TTL aggregation. Public interfaces and JSON configuration stay unchanged.

### Normal-configuration reproduction

Use an ordinary HTTP inbound and a freedom outbound with `streamSettings.sockopt.domainStrategy: "UseIPv4"`. The relevant DNS settings are:

```json
{
  "dns": {
    "queryStrategy": "UseIPv4",
    "enableParallelQuery": false,
    "servers": [
      {
        "address": "tcp+local://127.0.0.1:15353",
        "timeoutMs": 300,
        "serveStale": true,
        "serveExpiredTTL": 1
      },
      {
        "address": "tcp+local://127.0.0.1:15354",
        "timeoutMs": 300,
        "disableCache": true
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Two controlled loopback DNS-over-TCP peers and a loopback HTTP origin make the sequence repeatable:

1. The primary returns the origin's IP with TTL 1, priming the cache.
2. After 1.15 seconds, an HTTP request receives the stale answer and starts a refresh. The primary delays this refresh by six seconds, then returns SERVFAIL; the fallback remains healthy.
3. After another 1.2 seconds, the stale answer is no longer eligible. A new request joins the refresh, despite having only a 300 ms nameserver budget.

| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Serial DNS, HTTP request | 4,804 ms | 328 ms |
| Parallel DNS, HTTP request | 4,813 ms | 326 ms |
| Serial DNS, UDP DNS outbound request | 4,805 ms | 304 ms |
| Parallel DNS, UDP DNS outbound request | 4,800 ms | 301 ms |

issues.title: feat: follow server IP changes behind the host name without a manual reconnect
issues.body:
### Problem

A WireGuard/AWG config can name the server by host name (`Endpoint = vpn.example.com:443`). The client resolves that name **once per connection** and keeps using the resulting IP. When the address behind the name changes, every connected device keeps sending to the old IP and stays offline until the user toggles the tunnel by hand.

This happens in practice when:

- a self-hosted server fails over to a standby: the DNS record is switched to the standby, which has the same keys;
- a server is moved to another hosting or region and the DNS record is updated;
- the server has a dynamic IP behind DDNS;
- the provider changes the server's IP during maintenance.

In all these cases the server side cannot fix it, and the user often doesn't understand why "the VPN is connected but nothing works".

Why nothing recovers today (checked against `dev` @ 3121775 and `amneziawg-apple` @ bdaf0b3):

| Platform | Where the name is resolved | What happens later |
|---|---|---|
| Windows / Linux / macOS (daemon) | `WireguardProtocol::startMzImpl()` overwrites `hostName` in `m_rawConfig` with the IP | Reconnects on `networkChanged` / `wakeup` call `start()` again, but the config already holds the IP, so they reuse the old address |
| Android | `parseInetAddress()` in `Wireguard.configWireguard()` | `reconnectVpn()` reuses the saved `WireguardConfig` with the resolved address |
| iOS | `WireGuardAdapter.start()` → `resolvePeers()` | `didReceivePathUpdate()` → `endpointUapiConfiguration()` re-resolves the **already resolved IP** (`resolvedEndpoints`) for NAT64 synthesis, not the host name |
| macOS (NE) | same as iOS | path updates only call `wgBumpSockets()` |

The engine cannot recover on its own either:

- **No re-resolution.** `amneziawg-go` never resolves names. After `MaxHandshakeAttempts` it gives up until the next outgoing packet.
- **No roaming.** Android and iOS call `DisableSomeRoamingForBrokenMobileSemantics()`, so a packet from a new source address doesn't move the endpoint. Even without that, stateful NAT drops packets from an address the device didn't contact.

### Solution

Detect a tunnel that is up on the device but no longer reaches its server, then resolve the configured host name again. The detection rule is the one from wireguard-tools' [`contrib/reresolve-dns`](https://git.zx2c4.com/wireguard-tools/tree/contrib/reresolve-dns/reresolve-dns.sh): **the latest handshake is older than a rekey cycle while the device keeps sending to the peer.**

A live session with traffic or PersistentKeepalive renews its handshake every 120 s (`REKEY_AFTER_TIME`); a failed renewal is retried for 90 s more (`REKEY_ATTEMPT_TIME`). So "no handshake for 180 s and tx grew during that window" means the server is unreachable.

An idle tunnel without keepalive never handshakes and sends nothing, so it is never treated as stale. Before the first handshake, the age is counted from the tunnel start.

The same small state machine is implemented on every platform. It is pure logic with no I/O, and the C++ version is unit-tested:

- `client/core/utils/endpointWatchdog.{h,cpp}` — desktop, with `client/tests/testEndpointWatchdog.cpp`
- `client/android/wireguard/.../EndpointWatchdog.kt`
- `client/platforms/ios/EndpointWatchdog.swift`

It also rate-limits refreshes: the delay doubles after each attempt and resets on the next successful handshake.

#### Desktop (Windows, Linux, macOS with daemon)

- `WireguardProtocol` keeps the host names exactly as configured and resolves them on **every** `start()`. This alone makes the existing reconnects on network change and wakeup follow DNS changes.
- If resolution fails at start, the last address that worked is used, so a short DNS outage right after the old tunnel went down (e.g. with the kill switch on) doesn't break the reconnect.
- While the tunnel is up and the endpoint is a host name, `WireguardProtocol` polls `checkStatus()` every 20 s.
- The daemon's `status` reply gets an optional `lastHandshake` field

## Summary

Preserve an explicitly configured non-empty MTU when importing an Amnezia `vpn://` configuration. The WireGuard or AmneziaWG protocol default is now applied only when the imported MTU is missing or empty.

## Problem

`ImportController::processAmneziaConfig()` unconditionally replaced the MTU contained in imported WireGuard and AmneziaWG configurations with the protocol default. As a result, profiles that intentionally specified a custom MTU silently changed during import.

## Changes

- Keep a non-empty imported MTU unchanged.
- Treat whitespace-only MTU values as empty.
- Preserve the existing WireGuard/AmneziaWG default fallback for missing or empty values.

## Backward compatibility

Profiles without an MTU continue to receive the same protocol default. The change only affects profiles that already provide an explicit value.

## Verification

- Built the Windows x64 client and service in Release mode against `dev` at [`94b51df2`](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/commit/94b51df24790bf52427afe82d81c87a95460bdfd) (`5.0.3.1`) with this change included.
- Confirmed with `git range-diff` that the rebase preserves the patch without changing its contents.
- Before this rebase, imported a real `vpn://` profile on Windows and verified that its non-default MTU survives import. The MTU-handling implementation is unchanged.

## Related pull requests

- This is complementary to #3065, which changes the AmneziaWG default MTU value. This PR only changes when the default is applied.

Android: auto-reconnect when the AmneziaWG tunnel stalls after idle (connection watchdog)
issues.body:
AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.1 (AWG 3.1), Android 16, OnePlus 15.
Self-hosted AmneziaWG, mobile network (Russia), battery set
to "Unrestricted" for AmneziaVPN.

Problem
After the phone has been idle with the screen off, the tunnel
sometimes stalls: nothing works (Telegram, browser) until I
manually disconnect and reconnect in AmneziaVPN. It happens
several times a day. A manual reconnect always fixes it
immediately.

What we see on the server side
We captured traffic on our server during these episodes. While
the tunnel is stalled, no packets from the phone reach the server
at all — no handshake initiation, nothing, for 4–44 minutes.
Other devices on the same server work normally at the same time.
Typical sequence: the phone wakes up, sends a few data packets
with the old session from a new NAT port (the mobile operator
changed it during sleep), the server drops them (keys older than
180 s), and then the phone never sends a new handshake. A manual
reconnect opens a new socket, the handshake completes in ~0.1 s,
and traffic flows right away.

Feature request: connection watchdog
An option to detect a stalled tunnel and restart it automatically,
for example:
- if the latest handshake is older than ~140 s
  (REKEY_AFTER_TIME + KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT + REKEY_TIMEOUT, as in
  wireguard-tools reresolve-dns) while the app has traffic to send,
  or
- if a periodic check through the tunnel (ping/HTTP) fails
  N times in a row,
then recreate the socket and re-handshake — the same as a manual
reconnect. Configurable interval and on/off switch.

Similar features exist in other clients: WG Tunnel ("Restart
tunnel on ping failure"), mihomo-based clients (fallback groups
with health checks).

Server-side keepalive does not help here: we tried
PersistentKeepalive 25 on the server for this peer — the server
cannot reach the phone after the operator's NAT mapping changes,
only the phone can recover by sending first.

Thank you for AmneziaVPN!

issues.title: Windows: AmneziaVPN recreates incorrect local routes and breaks VPN sharing via Mobile Hotspot
issues.body:
# Bug Report: AmneziaVPN recreates incorrect local routes on Windows and breaks VPN Internet sharing via Mobile Hotspot

## Summary

When AmneziaVPN connects on Windows, it creates four local IPv4 routes on the `AmneziaVPN` interface with `RouteMetric = 0` and `Protocol = NetMgmt`. These routes take precedence over the correct local routes and interfere with Windows network routing.

In my configuration, this breaks Internet sharing through Windows Mobile Hotspot. The laptop can access the Internet through the VPN, but the connected Android phone cannot reliably access websites through the VPN.

Manually removing the four routes restores correct local routing and allows both the laptop and the phone to access the Internet through the VPN. However, the routes are recreated when AmneziaVPN reconnects.

## Environment

- Operating system: Windows 10, version 22H2
- VPN client: AmneziaVPN 5.0.4.2 prerelease
- VPN protocol: AmneziaWG
- VPN server: Self-hosted
- Network connection: Ethernet
- Ethernet adapter: Realtek, interface alias `Ethernet 5`
- Mobile Hotspot: Windows Mobile Hotspot using Microsoft Wi-Fi Direct Virtual Adapter
- Hotspot adapter alias: `Подключение по локальной сети* 10`
- VPN adapter alias: `AmneziaVPN`
- VPN adapter IPv4 address: `10.8.1.2`
- Ethernet IPv4 address: `192.168.0.167`
- Hotspot IPv4 address: `192.168.137.1`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Connect the laptop to the Internet through Ethernet.
2. Connect AmneziaVPN using the AmneziaWG protocol.
3. Enable Windows Mobile Hotspot.
4. Configure Internet Connection Sharing (ICS) on the `AmneziaVPN` adapter, sharing the connection with `Подключение по локальной сети* 10`.
5. Connect an Android phone to the hotspot.
6. Inspect the IPv4 routing table:

   ```powershell
   Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 |
   Where-Object {
       $_.InterfaceAlias -eq 'AmneziaVPN' -and
       $_.DestinationPrefix -in @(
           '192.168.0.0/24',
           '192.168.0.167/32',
           '192.168.137.0/24',
           '192.168.137.1/32'
       )
   } |
   Format-Table DestinationPrefix, NextHop, InterfaceAlias, RouteMetric, Protocol -Auto
   ```

7. Check the selected routes:

   ```powershell
   Find-NetRoute -RemoteIPAddress 192.168.0.1
   Find-NetRoute -RemoteIPAddress 192.168.137.1
   ```

8. Disconnect and reconnect AmneziaVPN and inspect the routing table again.

## Actual behavior

AmneziaVPN creates the following routes on interface `AmneziaVPN`:

| Destination prefix | Next hop | Route metric | Protocol |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `192.168.0.0/24` | `0.0.0.0` | 0 | NetMgmt |
| `192.168.0.167/32` | `0.0.0.0` | 0 | NetMgmt |
| `192.168.137.0/24` | `0.0.0.0` | 0 | NetMgmt |
| `192.168.137.1/32` | `0.0.0.0` | 0 | NetMgmt |

Windows then selects `AmneziaVPN` for traffic to local addresses that should be reached through the Ethernet or hotspot interface.

Observed results:

- `Find-NetRoute -RemoteIPAddress 192.168.0.1` selects `AmneziaVPN` instead of `Ethernet 5`.
- `Find-NetRoute -RemoteIPAddress 192.168.137.1` selects `AmneziaVPN` instead of `Подключение по локальной сети* 10`.
- `ping 192.168.0.1` times out.
- `ping 192.168.137.1` returns `General failure`.
- The laptop can still access websites through the VPN, while the Android phone connected to the hotspot cannot reliably access the Internet through the VPN.

After manually removing these four routes, Windows selects the correct interfaces and both the laptop and phone can access the Internet through the VPN.

After disconnecting and reconnecting AmneziaVPN, all four routes reappear.

## Expected behavior

AmneziaVPN should not install VPN routes that override the local connected routes required for Ethernet connectivity and Windows Mobile Hotspot / Internet Connection Sharing.

Local network and hotspot traffic should continue to use their respective local interfaces while Internet traffic is routed through the VPN.

Reconnecting the VPN should not reintroduce incorrect routes that break local connectivity or VPN Intern

issues.title: KillSwitch deadlocks network and client on suspend/resume on Linux
issues.body:
### Bug Report: KillSwitch deadlocks network and client on suspend/resume on Linux

  Environment:

  • OS: Linux (Debian 13, kernel 6.12, Wayland/Sway / any DE)
  • Amnezia version: 4.x / latest
  • Protocol: AmneziaWG (AWG) with KillSwitch enabled

  Steps to reproduce:

  1. Connect to any server using AmneziaWG with KillSwitch (route all traffic) enabled.
  2. Put laptop to sleep (suspend / close lid) for ~15 seconds.
  3. Wake up the laptop (open lid).

  Actual behavior:

  1. Wi-Fi reconnects to the local network, but there is zero internet access on the
  entire system.
  2. Amnezia GUI enters an infinite loop: "Reconnecting..." (Переподключение...).
  3. Killing the GUI process (pkill -9 AmneziaVPN) immediately clears the KillSwitch
  and restores network connectivity.

  Root cause analysis from logs:

  1. In AmneziaVPN-service, LinuxNetworkWatcherWorker detects NM interface property
  changes on wake, but completely ignores the link drop because the AP didn't change:
    [DEBUG] AmneziaVPN LinuxNetworkWatcherWorker : Properties changed for interface org.freedesktop.NetworkManager.Device.Wireless
    [DEBUG] AmneziaVPN LinuxNetworkWatcherWorker : Access point did not changed. Ignoring the changes

  2. The GUI client attempts to activate the VPN tunnel immediately upon resume before
  DHCP lease / default gateway on Wi-Fi is ready (which takes 3–5 seconds).
  3. The daemon inserts KillSwitch iptables rules (amnvpn.100.blockAll, amnvpn.310.blockDNS), but the handshake packets to the VPN endpoint fail because there is no
  route yet.
  4. The client's Qt state machine gets stuck in a handshake wait loop (polling every
  250ms), while the KillSwitch blocks all traffic and DNS on the machine.

  Suggested fix:

  1. Implement support for org.freedesktop.login1.Manager.PrepareForSleep (systemd
  inhibitor lock) to cleanly suspend/pause the tunnel before sleep.
  2. On resume, wait for default route / network gateway availability before re-
  engaging KillSwitch and handshake attempts.
  3. Add a timeout / reset logic in the GUI client to avoid unrecoverable
  "Reconnecting..." state.

issues.title: fix(scripts): start server units after network-online.target
issues.body:
The systemd units written by `install_server.sh` only order after `network.target`. That target means the network stack is configured, not that the network is up, so on some boots the server starts before DNS works.

The server resolves hostnames while it loads its config. One example is the realm STUN servers. When that lookup fails at boot, the service exits with:

```
FATAL failed to load server config {"error": "invalid config: realm.stun: lookup <stun host>: i/o timeout"}
```

The unit has no `Restart=`, so it stays down until someone starts it by hand.

This change adds `Wants=network-online.target` and `After=network-online.target` to the server unit template, which systemd documents for services that need a working network at startup: https://systemd.io/NETWORK_ONLINE/
